name: Seaweed oligosaccharides

lead: Seaweed oligosaccharides are short sugar chains from brown seaweed such as Laminaria digitata, marketed as a topical ingredient for acne-prone skin, alone or as a zinc complex. The aim is a calmer, more balanced skin surface and fewer blemishes.

The main source is a 2013 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Science, which frames them as a marine-derived addition to benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics and retinoids as topical acne treatments. No further trial data were found, and detailed mechanisms are not given.

paras: They are used as a complementary topical ingredient in skincare, alongside standard acne products.
No safety data are cited, and effects on acne are not well characterized.

angle.text: Seaweed oligosaccharides are marine-derived sugars applied to acne-prone skin to calm the skin surface and reduce blemishes. They are marketed as a complementary ingredient, and the support is a single literature review.

lead: Seaweed oligosaccharides are short carbohydrate chains derived from the polysaccharide cell wall of brown seaweed, notably Laminaria digitata (oarweed), studied as a topical, marine-derived ingredient for acne.[1][2] A published review also describes a seaweed oligosaccharide-zinc complex (SOZC).[1]

The review, a 2013 article in the Journal of Cosmetic Science, presents them as a possible addition to benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics and retinoids as mainstay topical acne treatments.[1] Beyond that review, the sources used here contain little human data.

paras: L. digitata is a large brown alga of the northern Atlantic, harvested mostly to make alginic acid and also used in some cosmetics.[2] The oligosaccharides discussed for acne are derived from its polysaccharide membrane.[1]

The 2013 review examined the available literature on seaweed oligosaccharides and on the SOZC complex as topical acne ingredients.[1] The abstract available does not give trial sizes or results, so effects are not summarized here. Patent filings describe fermented preparations containing seaweed oligosaccharides, which are not clinical evidence.[3][4]
No registered or published clinical trials were found in the sources used here beyond the literature review described above.[1]
